questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: What a contract leaves unstated
questions.learningObjective: name the part of a promise a contract does not make
questions.stem: A lookup routine promises that it returns record identifiers in ascending order, and its test sorts what came back and compares the result with a sorted copy of the input. The test passes on a case holding two records that both carry the identifier 41. What does that show about the contract?

options.text: No clause fixes which of the two records with the same identifier comes first, so the pass proves order only
The order for equal identifiers is fixed as written, and the test is simply not strict enough to notice
options.misconception: assumes a clause about ascending order also settles equal identifiers

options.text: The routine returns duplicates, which is the only reason two records share an identifier in the result
options.misconception: reads a shared identifier in the output as a duplication defect

options.text: The test is at fault for sorting a copy rather than the original list of identifiers
options.misconception: blames the test harness instead of the missing clause

questions.explanation: A contract is the set of promises a caller may rely on, and a promise about ascending order is already satisfied by either arrangement of two equal keys, so nothing in it fixes the tie. Sorting a copy and comparing lists can only confirm the clause that was written, which makes a pass on a tied case evidence about ordering and not about tie-breaking. Relying on the tie is relying on something nobody agreed, and it breaks the first time the implementation is rewritten.
questions.hint: Ask whether ascending order says anything about two equal keys.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Which clause a caller breaks
questions.learningObjective: tell a precondition failure from a postcondition failure
questions.stem: A routine publishes two clauses: the caller must pass an index between 0 and the length minus one, and the routine returns the item at that index without changing the list. A caller passes the length, and the routine throws. Which clause did that caller break?

options.text: The precondition, because the value it supplied is one the published clause excludes
The postcondition, because no item came back at the index the caller chose
options.misconception: blames a missing result on the caller rather than on the input it chose

options.text: Neither clause, because a routine may always refuse an input it does not like
options.misconception: treats any refusal as covered by the contract

options.text: The postcondition, because leaving the list unchanged is the promise in question
options.misconception: mistakes the non-mutation clause for the one at fault

questions.explanation: A precondition is the caller's half of the contract: the condition that must hold before the call is made, and whose violation is the caller's own fault. Here the value supplied falls outside the stated range, so the caller broke it and a throw is the correct response rather than a broken promise. A postcondition is the routine's half, describing what is true afterwards, and it is the routine that is answerable for it.
questions.hint: Ask who is answerable for the condition before the call.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A contract no implementation can meet
questions.learningObjective: detect a pair of clauses that cannot both hold
questions.stem: A withdrawal routine promises two things: the returned balance is never negative, and every withdrawal reduces the balance by exactly the amount requested. An account holds 40 and a caller requests 60. What does that combination tell you?

options.text: No implementation can satisfy both clauses for this call, because the only balance fitting them is one the account cannot hold
Nothing, because refusing the call leaves the balance unchanged and so satisfies both promises at once
options.misconception: believes a refusal discharges a clause about reducing the balance

options.text: Nothing, because a clause stays unenforced until a caller actually objects to it
options.misconception: assumes a written promise can be ignored until someone complains

options.text: The precondition is at fault, since the balance held was never part of what the caller passed in
options.misconception: looks for the fault in an input clause rather than in the two promises

questions.explanation: Clauses are read together, so a contract can be unsatisfiable even when each clause reads sensibly alone: a balance cannot both stay at or above zero and fall by 60 from 40. That is a defect in the specification, and it is detectable from the text before any code is written, which makes it far cheaper to find here than in a report from a user. Refusing the call satisfies the first clause and breaks the second, so a refusal does not rescue the pair.
questions.hint: Read the two promises together and ask whether any balance fits both.

questions.topic: A contract written only in prose
questions.learningObjective: judge what a length check can and cannot establish
questions.stem: A module's entire contract is one sentence: the routine returns the rows in order. Its only test builds a list, calls the routine, and checks that the result has the same length as the list it passed in. What does that test leave unproved?

options.text: That the rows come back in order, because a comparison of lengths cannot see order at all
That the result holds rows, because a matching length establishes what the values are
options.misconception: believes a length check pins down the type of what came back

options.text: That the call is cheap, because a passing test shows how little work the routine did
options.misconception: reads a passing test as a statement about cost

options.text: That the routine terminates, because a loop that never ended would produce no result
options.misconception: believes a length check is evidence about termination

questions.explanation: A test can only establish the clause it exercises, and comparing two lengths never inspects the arrangement of the elements. The single promise in the contract is order and the test exercises cardinality, so the one clause the module owes is the one clause the test leaves open. Writing the promise in prose does not help either, because prose cannot fail a build: only a test that inspects positions, or a type that makes the wrong order unrepresentable, turns a sentence into something a machine can catch.

questions.topic: An interface with one method too many
questions.learningObjective: price an addition to a shared interface
questions.stem: A shared interface has grown from 5 methods to 11 over a year. Three teams implement it and a fourth is planned, and every method added has at least one caller. What does the eleventh method cost?

options.text: Every implementation must supply and test it, so each addition multiplies the work across implementers
One extra line of text, which each implementer already has a place to write
options.misconception: treats an interface method as a cost paid once by the author

options.text: Nothing extra, because callers are built against the interface rather than the implementations
options.misconception: believes the abstract type shields implementers from the addition

options.text: A single method, since a new implementation can inherit the ten the others already have
options.misconception: assumes an implementation can inherit a method it does not provide

questions.learningObjective: read the readability cost of optional flags
questions.stem: A method now takes four optional boolean parameters and a delimiter string, added one at a time over three years. A call site reads export(rows, true, ',', false, 'utf-8'). What does that call site show about the contract?

options.text: A caller must know the position and meaning of every argument, and no call shows which combination was meant
That the defaults are wrong, since most callers are now passing values of their own
options.misconception: blames the default values for a problem the positions cause

options.text: That the method has grown slow, since five arguments are read on every single export
options.misconception: reads argument count as a cost paid on each call

questions.topic: Who may change a published contract
questions.learningObjective: name who holds authority over a published promise
questions.stem: A library is used by 30 teams, and a change would alter the value an existing method returns for the three teams that call it. The author wants to ship it in the next patch release. Who has to approve it?

options.text: The library's owner, because a change to a published promise is not the author's private choice
Nobody, since a patch release may never change what a method returns
options.misconception: believes the version label already settles what a release may hold

options.text: Only the three teams that call the method, since the other 27 are unaffected by it
options.misconception: assumes the affected callers hold the decision rather than the owner

options.text: The teams that asked for the change, since they are the ones carrying its risk
options.misconception: hands approval to the requesters rather than to the owner

In a shared library the owner is usually a named maintainer or a small group, and the reason is accountability: someone has to know which callers exist, judge the migration window and carry the announcement. A patch label is not permission to move a promise.

questions.topic: What a major number means
questions.learningObjective: identify the version part that records a removal
questions.stem: Version 2.0.0 of a library removes a method that 12 of 40 dependent services call. Which part of the version number accounts for that removal, and what does it tell a caller in advance?

options.text: The major number, which warns a caller that existing calls may no longer work as written
The minor number, which announces a new feature that keeps old calls working
options.misconception: reads a removal as an addition in a compatible release

options.text: The patch number, which records a defect fixed with nothing else altered
options.misconception: treats a removal as a repair rather than a change of promise

options.text: None of the three, since a removal matters only once old code fails to compile
options.misconception: believes a removal is harmless while anything still runs

Nothing, because no behaviour changed and only the shape of the call is different

questions.stem: Version 1.4.2 fixes a date parser that used to reject 31 February, and the fix now rolls that date into 1 March. Three services store the dates the parser produces. What does the patch number fail to record?

options.text: Only the failure count, since a fix reduces errors without changing results

questions.learningObjective: explain the cost of an unearned major number
questions.stem: A library jumped from 1.9.0 to 2.0.0 with no change to any public call, purely to signal a new direction. The team now wants 2.1.0 to carry a real breaking change. What problem has the first bump created?

options.text: A major number that no longer marks a break, so the teams that read the first will doubt the next
Only a gap in the history, since 1.9.0 and 2.0.0 are not consecutive releases
options.misconception: treats the cost as a matter of numbering tidiness

options.text: Only a naming problem, since the words major and minor mean nothing to whoever reads them
options.misconception: believes the labels carry no shared meaning to depend on

It names no replacement, so a caller cannot move even if it chooses to move

options.text: It sits in the source rather than the release notes, so most callers will never see it

options.misconception: objects to the granularity rather than to the missing date

questions.stem: An engineer must use a module written by another team, and the source runs to 1,200 lines with no comments. Their plan is to read the whole implementation from top to bottom before calling anything. What is wrong with that plan?

The body is longer than the contract, so the contract is the better use of an hour
options.misconception: judges by line count rather than by what a caller must know

options.misconception: believes a contract page is always longer than the code

questions.stem: A module promises to save a row. Its own documentation says the caller must call prepare() once before the first save of each session, because the module writes to a single open file handle. What does that promise cost the caller?

Nothing, because a documented step is already part of the module's own job
options.misconception: believes writing a requirement down removes it from callers

options.text: Only the extra call, since prepare() costs a caller nothing beyond the line of code
options.misconception: counts the visible line and ignores the records at risk

A place to change later, so the cost is only paid if the call is ever redirected
options.misconception: defers the cost of the indirection to a hypothetical future

questions.topic: The limited value of a generated page
questions.learningObjective: explain what generation guarantees and what it leaves to a person
questions.stem: A library's reference page is generated from annotated source in the same build as the code, and a renamed method updates the page in the same commit. Explain why the page cannot be wrong about names, and what a reader still has to be told by hand.

answer.exemplar: The page is produced by reading the same declarations the compiler reads, so a name that no longer exists cannot appear on it and a declared name cannot be missing from it. That class of documentation error is removed by construction rather than by anyone's care, which is the real gain. What survives generation is everything the declarations do not say: why a value is refused, which failures are expected, what a caller must arrange before the first call, what the method is not for, and what changed in the last release and why. Those sentences have to be written by someone who knows the intent, reviewed by someone who uses the method, and dated so a reader can tell a stale sentence from a current one.

questions.explanation: Generated pages remove one whole class of documentation error, which is a real and limited gain: names, signatures and types cannot drift because they are read from the same text the build compiles. The temptation is to treat that as proof the page is adequate, and a reader who trusts it that way finds no statement of why a method refuses an out-of-range value, of what must be true first, or of what a recent change altered. Intent and history are written by people, and a hand-written section can be as wrong as anything else.
questions.hint: Ask what the generator reads from, and what it never sees.

questions.topic: Two kinds of review comment
questions.learningObjective: explain why a defect comment and a taste comment need different handling
questions.stem: A reviewer writes 'I would call this token rather than item', and in the same request writes 'this loop can read one past the end of the list'. Explain why the two comments should be handled differently, and what each one costs.

answer.exemplar: The second names an input, an operation and an outcome, so it identifies something the change does incorrectly and the author has to resolve it by fixing the bound or by showing it cannot be reached. The first names a preference between two equally clear names, and the author is entitled to keep the one they have. The costs differ the same way: a defect comment costs a rewrite of the author's time and is worth it, because the alternative is a fault in production. A preference comment costs the reviewer a sentence and the author a distraction, and enough of them turn a review into something nobody reads carefully. A workable rule is that a comment obliges a change only when the author could point to something the change does wrongly, and everything else is labelled as taste so it can be declined without argument.

questions.explanation: A review comment is worth acting on when it identifies something the change does incorrectly, and a bound that can be read past is that. A naming preference identifies nothing wrong, and the distinction matters because the author's response differs: one requires a decision about the code, the other requires none. The cost side matters too, because a review that mixes the two trains its author to read every comment as an objection, which is the fastest way to stop a real defect from being fixed.
questions.hint: Ask which comment names something the change does wrongly.

questions.stem: Three teams each own a third of a service whose shared client library is being rewritten, and each has a working client to keep running. Explain what has to be settled before any team writes code, and what goes wrong if only the method names are settled.

answer.exemplar: They have to settle more than names. The names and the order of the arguments must be fixed, because a call written against one order and compiled against another fails late and confusingly. They must settle which failures are possible and what each one means, since a caller who cannot name a failure cannot handle it. They must settle what the library promises about time, about whether a result may change underneath a caller, and about whether a returned value may be kept. And they must settle who owns the surface, because somebody has to settle the argument when each side finds a case the other never thought of. If only the names are agreed, the teams do not really run in parallel: each invents its own expectation of the failures, of the ordering of results and of whether a returned list is stable, and the first integration run becomes the first time anyone compares them.

questions.explanation: Parallel work on an agreed surface is cheaper than working separately only if the surface is agreed well enough that two implementations can be written without talking. Names are the smallest part of that, and the parts that cost the most to discover late are the ones nobody writes down: the failure cases, the treatment of ordering, and who may hold a returned value. A one-line agreement of names leaves each team to invent the rest, and those disagreements surface during integration, when they are most expensive to unpick.
questions.hint: Ask which parts of a surface a name does not cover.

questions.topic: Green tests and a broken caller
questions.learningObjective: explain how a reviewed and tested change can still break a consumer
questions.stem: A team changes a shared paging helper so a page of results can never be empty, and it passes review with the whole suite green. Three weeks later two consumers report missing rows. Explain how both results can be true, and what evidence would have shown the risk.

answer.exemplar: Every one of those checks is local to the repository, and the failure is not. The paging helper is public, so the consumers that broke sit in other repositories, and the review could only see the calls inside this one, which still pass. The suite could only assert what it had chosen to assert, and nothing in it was written to say that a page is never empty, so the change moved the contract without contradicting a single assertion. What would have helped is evidence about the surface rather than the code: a published contract that states what an exhausted page returns, a record of who called the helper that was current when the change was made, a test that pins the empty case, and a route by which such a change reaches whoever owns the contract. A count of the new failures narrows the search afterwards, but it cannot say which consumer to go and ask.

questions.explanation: A change can be correct, reviewed and green and still break a consumer, because review and tests both only see the repository they run in, while a published helper is used by code nobody in that room can reach. The change moved a promise without altering a name, a type or a single assertion, so nothing local had a reason to fail. The remedy is not more of the same review but evidence about the surface: what the contract promises for an exhausted page, who its callers are, and which of them depends on the old behaviour.
questions.hint: Ask which callers the checks in that repository could see.
